question: How many cups of tea do people in the United Kingdom drink per day?

target.what: Total number of cups of tea consumed by people in the United Kingdom per day, counting all tea-drinking occasions (cups/mugs of tea, including from tea bags, loose leaf, and prepared tea), averaged over a representative day in the most recent period before the cutoff
target.publisher: No single official publisher; constructed from industry (UK Tea & Infusions Association), survey (Defra/NatCen), and retail data
target.cadence: Irregular; industry and survey estimates published sporadically
target.caveats: Ambiguity between cups of tea (hot tea from leaves/bags) versus all tea-based drinks (iced tea, RTD, herbal infusions). assessment.note: Both are the same ITC/UKTIA-derived figure (100m cups/day and 36bn cups/year); 36bn/365 ≈ 98.6m, so they are internally consistent but not independent — one underlying source.

ITC/UKTIA ~100m cups/day vs Kantar 18.3bn tea-drinking occasions/year (~50m/day). Different definitions (cups vs occasions; Kantar household panel may exclude out-of-home and multiple cups per occasion), so a real scope gap rather than a pure contradiction; the gap is the main uncertainty to resolve.

Physical-flow anchors: 113kt consumption (2015), 1.9 kg/capita (2015), and 72m kg/year (Statista, excl. herbal/RTD/instant). The 72m kg figure is lower than 113kt, consistent with decline and narrower scope; both usable with a grams-per-cup conversion.
UKTIA cup-frequency distribution (38% 1–2, 36% 3–4, 15% 5–6, 2% >11) sums to 91%, leaving ~9% for 7–11 and non-drinkers; internally coherent and supports a per-drinker mean of roughly 3–4 cups/day.
Crave/UKTIA distribution (35% 3–4, 44% 1–2, 20% 5–6) is a similar shape to p41–p44 but with different shares; same underlying survey family, so corroboration is weak (shared source).

p33 says >9 in 10 drink at least one cup/day; p53 says 98% drink tea daily. Both are implausibly high vs p117 (78% drink tea) and p41–p44 (9% non-drinkers); likely survey framing/definition differences. Treat as upper-bound context, not direct inputs.

Historical decline: 23 cups/person/week in 1974 and 68g/person/week in 1974 vs 22g now — consistent with a long-run fall in per-capita tea consumption; supports using a declining trend rather than a flat 100m.

methods.rationale: Physical-flow route: Statista's 72m kg/year (p62) divided by grams per cup (a1) gives cups/year, converted to cups/day. Independent of the UKTIA anchor. Failure modes: p62 excludes herbal/RTD/instant (slightly narrows scope) and may include non-beverage/industrial use; a1 uncertainty dominates.
methods.error: unit of the formula's result: 'kg/cup/day' (kg / cp / d) cannot be converted to 'cup/day' (cp / d). Write the unit the formula actually produces (an annual total gives a per-year result); code converts units, do not add scale factors

kept.name: Grams of tea per cup (hot brewed tea)
kept.rationale: Tea-bag and loose-leaf mass ranges (p188, p189, p192, p193) and UKTIA's 3 g conversion (p163) bracket 2-3 g; 2.5 g is the central value.
kept.applies_when: Converting UK tea mass (kg/year) to cups, assuming negligible waste and that bag mass approximates brewed leaf mass.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that typical UK cups use substantially more or less leaf (e.g., large-scale bag-weight audit outside 2-3 g).

kept.name: Share of UK population drinking tea on a given day
kept.rationale: Drinker-share estimates range from 78% (p117) to 98% (p53); the lower end is more plausible for a whole-population daily share, so 0.75 with a wide band.
kept.applies_when: Decomposing total cups as population x drinker share x cups per drinker.
kept.falsified_by: A representative all-ages survey showing daily drinker share outside 55-90%.

kept.name: Mean cups per tea drinker per day
kept.rationale: Frequency distributions (p41-p44, p34-p36) and the 35% three-or-more figure (p157/p196) imply a mean of roughly 2-3 cups among drinkers.
kept.applies_when: Decomposing total cups as population x drinker share x cups per drinker.
kept.falsified_by: A representative survey giving a mean cups-per-drinker clearly outside 1.5-3.2.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
